parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ama (“wetnurse”), from Late Latin amma, q.v.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin creātūra.

Borrowed from Late Latin ēvāsiōnem (literally “a going out, an escaping”), from Latin ēvāsus, perfect passive participle of ēvādō (“to escape, to go out”), from ē- (“out”) + vādō (“to go; to walk”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go”). Cognate with English wade.

parole.significato: knee (joint or the region of the joint in the middle part of the leg between the thigh and the shank)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish ynojo, from Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.

parole.significato: a louse, a cootie (a kind of parasitic insect, lice)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pioio, from Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus, from pēdis, from Proto-Indo-European *pezd-. Compare Portuguese piolho. Doublet of pedículo.

parole.significato: sisterhood (the idea of universal experience amongst women, regardless of other traits or factors)
parole.testo: From Renaissance Late Latin sorōritātem, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. Akin to Portuguese sororidade, French sororité, English sorority.
Inherited from Old Spanish suegra (“mother-in-law”), from Late Latin socra, from Latin socrus, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱrúh₂, whence German Schwieger/schwieger- and Russian Свекровь (Svekrovʹ).
Inherited from Old Spanish suegro, from Late Latin socrus m, from Latin socer, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱrúh₂.

parole.significato: great-great-grandchild; great-great-grandson (great-great-granddaughter for the feminine form)
parole.testo: From tras- + Old Spanish trasnieto (“great-grandchild”), from tras- + nieto (“grandson”), formed from nieta (“granddaughter”), from Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis, from Proto-Indo-European *néptih₂. Compare Latin nepōs (“grandson, grandaughter, nephew, niece”) (genitive singular nepōtis).
Borrowed from Late Latin vīrulentus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wisós (“poison; slime; fluidity”).
Inherited from Late Latin nonnus. Compare Italian nonno (“grandfather”).
